spec.title: Evidence from a raw export
spec.intro:
You are handed a raw access export and asked to produce a one-file piece of evidence
answering a control question — plus a record of any collection problems — and to make
the whole thing re-runnable. This terminal is a real simulation of the lab box: the
commands you run here produce the same results they would on the machine itself.
Start by provisioning your lab files.

tasks.instruction:
Before touching anything, ask the shell where you are and what is around you:
run `pwd`, then `ls`. Read the prompt first and predict both answers.

hints.nudge: Two of the three orientation questions from §4.2 — where am I, and what's around me?

tasks.explain:
The prompt was telling you the answer to `pwd` the whole time — `~` is your home
directory, `/home/analyst`. Orientation is the first discipline: when evidence
collection goes wrong, "where was I standing?" is the first audit question.

tasks.instruction:
Provision the lab: run `lab-setup 01`. Then practice the three forms of movement —
enter `lab01` with a relative path, return home with bare `cd`, and come back into
`lab01` using its absolute path.

hints.nudge: A relative path starts from where you stand; an absolute path starts from `/`. `cd` with nothing always goes home.

hints.concept: §4.2 — the filesystem is a tree, and you are always standing somewhere in it

hints.reveal: lab-setup 01, then: cd lab01 · cd · cd /home/analyst/lab01

tasks.explain:
Both routes ended in the same place — a relative path is directions from here,
an absolute path is directions from the root. Evidence scripts use absolute paths
precisely because they can't assume where the runner is standing.

tasks.instruction:
Using `cat`, `grep`, and `wc` connected only by pipes, produce the count of access
rows that grant a role containing the word "admin". No single tool that "does it
all" — the point is composition.

hints.nudge: Which program emits the file? Which keeps only the lines you care about? Which counts what's left?

hints.concept: §4.3 — the pipe connects one program's stdout to the next program's stdin

tasks.explain:
Three small honest tools and two pipes just evaluated an access-control claim.
That number — and not a screenshot of a spreadsheet — is the atomic unit of
continuous assurance: text in, text out, re-runnable next quarter.

tasks.instruction:
Re-run your pipeline, but redirect the count into `~/lab01/evidence-admin-count.txt`.
Then confirm the file holds exactly that number — without re-running the pipeline.

hints.nudge: `>` points stdout somewhere other than your screen. Reading a file back is a job for the program that emits files.

hints.concept: §4.3 — redirection turns output you glance at into an artifact you keep

hints.reveal: cat access-export.csv | grep admin | wc -l > evidence-admin-count.txt, then: cat evidence-admin-count.txt

tasks.explain:
The count stopped being something you saw and became something you HAVE — a kept
artifact. That file is evidence in the audit sense: durable, inspectable, and
produced by a documented, re-runnable question.

tasks.instruction:
One row in the export is malformed, and the lab's parsing tool complains about it.
Rebuild your evidence using `parse-access-export` as the first stage of the
pipeline, capturing its complaint into `collection-errors.log` while keeping the
evidence file clean. The two files must end up containing different things.

hints.nudge: stdout and stderr are different channels. `>` only redirects one of them — which operator takes the other?

hints.concept: §4.3 — two output channels exist so results and complaints can go different places

hints.reveal: parse-access-export access-export.csv 2> collection-errors.log | grep admin | wc -l > evidence-admin-count.txt

tasks.explain:
Your evidence file is clean data; the operational complaint went to its own log a
human can review. That one line is a defensible evidence-collection step: the
answer AND an auditable record of what went wrong while collecting it.

tasks.instruction:
Run a `grep -q` form of your check against the export, then inspect `$?`.
State (in your notes) which exit code means the control PASSED for this question,
and why "no output" and "failed" are different facts.

hints.nudge: `-q` means quiet — grep says nothing and only sets the verdict. `$?` holds the previous program's exit code.

hints.concept: §4.4 — output is for people; the exit code is for machines

tasks.explain:
A machine just evaluated your control with zero human reading. For THIS question,
grep finding a match (exit 0) means admin grants exist — whether that's a pass or a
finding depends on the claim. The exit code is the hinge that makes monitoring
continuous instead of quarterly.

tasks.instruction:
Make it reproducible: put your working sequence into `check-admin-access.sh` (the
editor `nano` is on this box, or compose the file with redirection), make it
executable, and run it twice with the export as its argument. Both runs must
produce identical evidence.

hints.nudge: A script is just the lines you already typed, saved. `chmod +x` makes it runnable as `./check-admin-access.sh`.

hints.concept: §4.6 — automation is just memory; a saved sequence is a reproducible check

hints.reveal: nano check-admin-access.sh — paste your t5 pipeline with "$1" in place of the filename — then chmod +x check-admin-access.sh and ./check-admin-access.sh access-export.csv (twice)

tasks.explain:
It produced identical evidence twice — that is the difference between "we verified
this once last audit" and "we verify this continuously and can prove it." You just
built your first continuously-runnable control check; module 13 will put it on a
schedule and alert on drift.

tasks.instruction:
In 4–6 sentences: where were you standing and how did you know; why the pipe
composition worked; why stdout/stderr separation mattered; and what the exit code
meant. Write it as if explaining to a non-technical colleague — use the terminal's
origin story from §3, not jargon.

hints.nudge: The §3 mental model: terminal (dumb endpoint) → shell (REPL) → kernel → programs.

tools.lab-setup:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Lab provisioning tool (module 01 §6 setup). The CSV bytes are canon-locked to
# modules/01-terminal-and-command-line-basics/labs/setup.sh — a CI drift check asserts equality.
set -euo pipefail
case "${1:-}" in
  01)
    mkdir -p "$HOME/lab01"
    cat > "$HOME/lab01/access-export.csv" <<'CSV'
user,role
alice,admin
bob,viewer
carol,legacy-admin
dave,editor
erin,admin
frank,viewer
MALFORMED_ROW_WITH_NO_DELIMITER
grace,auditor
CSV
    echo "lab01 fixture written to $HOME/lab01/access-export.csv"
    ;;
  *)
    echo "usage: lab-setup <module-number>" >&2
    exit 1
    ;;
esac
tools.collect-encryption-status:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Fictional evidence collector from module 01 §5.2 (authored-fixture; stderr line is prose canon).
# stdout: one line per laptop. stderr: the unreachable-host complaint, verbatim from §5.2.
cat <<'OUT'
laptop-01: encrypted
laptop-02: encrypted
laptop-03: encrypted
laptop-04: encrypted
laptop-05: not-encrypted
OUT
echo "WARN: host db-07 unreachable" >&2
